msDesc.head: Thomas Waldensis, Doctrinale, pars II (liber V); England (?London), AD 1427 × 1431

msContents.summary: ¶ This stately manuscript is one of the finest in the collection and also one of the largest. The text itself is part of a vast enterprise by Thomas Netter of Walden (d. 1430), a statement of orthodoxy to answer the evangelical challenge of John Wyclif. As such, the manuscript was a significant object for the College to have possessed, a gift from the Founder to bolster his Fellows in their spiritual combat with Wycliffism. Netter was prior provincial of the Carmelite order and this copy was made by a Carmelite scribe, Reginald Westakyr, from a copy very close to an authorial exemplar. The manuscript was given to the College by the Founder, whose death came mere months after Netter’s own. Ours is the oldest copy of the work now extant and for its physical quality has been described as ‘among the finest known monastic productions of the fifteenth century’.

msItem.author: Thomas Netter of Walden OCarm
msItem.title: Doctrinale antiquitatum fidei, pars II (liber V): De sacramentis
msItem.note: Ed. Jodocus Badius Ascensius, pr. Paris 1521 (V), 1523 (VI), 1532 (I–IV), &c.; ed. B. Blanciotti, 3 vols (Venice 1757–9 / repr. Farnborough 1967); K. J. Alban, The Teaching and Impact of the ‘Doctrinale’ of Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1374–1430) (Turnhout 2010); Harvey, ‘Diffusion of the Doctrinale’, 289; Harvey, ‘Netter manuscripts and printings’, 148–56; Nichols, Seeable Signs, 120–22. The work divides at 2r (prologus), 18r (De sacramentis), 44r (De eukaristia), 207r (De baptismo), 239v (De confirmatione), 248v (De ordinatione), 279v (De coniuge), 289v (De penitencia), 352r (De unccione), 354r (epilogus). Loss of text with cancels between fols. 162 and 163, 191 and 192.
Fol. 357r. An erasure of three lines beneath the last line of writing; the remainder of col. a and col. b are blank.
Fol. 358. A half leaf, ruled but blank.
Fol. 359v. Three notes by Thomas Gascoigne, done at different times:

(i) liber quintus doctrinalis Antiquitatum ecclesie, editus a Magistro thoma Walden’ fratre carmelita et doctore sacre Theologie in studio vniuersitate studii oxoniensis creato, cuius nomen fuit nettar a (?)primeno (primo nominatus?) et bene quare fecit rete in quo capiuntur heretici, et fuit confessor henrici quinti et henrici sexti regum Anglie; et anglicus natiuitate fuit et rotomagi in [ erasure ] normannia obiit in die animarum Rege henrico sexto anglie, ibidem in morte sua existente et fuit ordinis carmelitarum fratrum sub regula degens sancti basilii episcopi et doctoris greci, sanctissimo Iero’ doctori contemporanei.

(ii) Anno domini 1446o obiit in villa byry dux glocestrie humfridus lancastyr, henrici iiij. regis filius, henrici quinti fratris, henrici vjti auunculi qui dotauit vniuersitatem oxon’ in communi libraria bonis et plurimis libris et scienciarum liberalium [legum et decretorum] et sacre theologie tam in originalibus sanctorum doctorum quam aliorum scolasticorum doctorum et postillatorum.
(iii) postillare est textum post textum, ordinate exponendo, inferre.

supportDesc.support: Parchment. Parchment is excellent: bright, clean and consistent, flexible with an even sit. It has a suede-like nap, barely distinguishable between sides. It has the hallmarks of London manufacture. Arranged like to like, flesh-side outermost, except for Q4 which goes hair-side outermost. There are remarkably few production flaws; the appearance is impeccable, but the following may be noted: scores and flay lines at 25, 126; production holes have been stitched and unpicked on 21 (in-text), 25, 238 (in-text), 270; holes, often gelatinized, in the margins of 9, 26, 38, 75, 79, 89, 91, 95, 122, 149, 170, 173, 193, 196, 219, 251, 256, 267, 275, 289; a trivial water stain at the head of 12 to 16. The book seems to have been left open for some time, 138v–139r being unusually dirty and discoloured, with many stains at the foot and ring-marks, as from a glue pot. The opening leaves at front and back are extensively wormed, expiring on fols. 13 and 336 respectively.
supportDesc.foliation: Foliated in early twentieth-century Bodleian pencil, incorporating Coxe’s sporadic numbering as usual. Foliation to 359, the penultimate leaf, a flyleaf, but skipping a leaf after 7, so really 359 plus 2 at the end.
supportDesc.collation: a (fols. i–ii; first formerly pastedown, second a stub) 12 (fols. 1–2) 28 (fols. 3–9, one skipped in the foliation after 7) 38 (fols. 10–18, plus one after eight) 4–218 (fols. 19–162) 228 (fols. 163–167, first to third cancelled with loss of text) 23–258 (fols. 168–191) 268 (fols. 192–198, first cancelled with loss of text) 27–468 (fols. 199–358, eighth is cut down) 472 (fols. 359–[360]). Catchwords are given by the scribe horizontally at text size underneath the second column; they are boxed in a hairline banderole, each made individually distinctive. A quire signature is visible at 94r, i.e. the fourth leaf of Q13, having the form ‘M iiij’, and ‘O iiij’ on 314r, Q41. Another hand wrote ‘N iiij’ in Q14. The positioning at the outer edge near the foot means that these have been cropped elsewhere.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled in brown lead for two columns of 45 lines, with an intercolumnar space of 16 mm. Vertical rules are single and pass to the edges; horizontal rules keep within the two columns of text, except for the two at top and bottom, which extend to the edges and cross the intercolumnar space. Margins are wide and generous. A turn-in on 223 shows the original margins to have been 25 mm wider. Prickings by awl are visible at the foot as guides for the vertical rules, and down the fore-edge in QQ13, 26, pricked through the prepared pile.

handDesc.handNote: Mostly the work of the Carmelite scribe Reginald Westakyr, who signed himself on 206v: ‘westakyr carmelite’. The signature comes at the end of the section De eucharistia, a common placement among Carmelite manuscripts of this date (Harvey, ‘Diffusion’, 282). He gave his full name elsewhere, in a colophon to a copy of De corpore et sanguine Domini by Lanfranc, part of a larger Carmelite eucharistic collection that is BnF MS lat. 2473: ‘Scriptum per religiosum Fratrem Reginaldum Westakyr, ordinis beate marie genetricis dei de monte Carmeli’ (fol. 81v); the manuscript was carried back to France by the provincial Laurent Bureau and given to the Carmelite studium generale in Paris in 1494 (as per an inscription on fol. 166r). Westakyr writes here a Textura semi-quadrata, soft in aspect and consistently made, with excellent line discipline. Another scribe writing a very similar hand supplied the three quires between fols. 207 and 230. Punctuation is by low point. Ink is mostly black, sometimes dark brown. Each scribe did his own rubrication. The wider context of Carmelite scribal production at this time, including Westakyr’s contribution, is considered by M. Parkes, Their Hands Before Our Eyes (London 2008), 28–30.

decoDesc.summary: The decorative scheme places our manuscript in a stylistically related group of four, all Carmelite copies of the Doctrinale: Lat. 106, BnF lat. 3378, Oxford, Magdalen College, lat. 157 (both written by Robert Freton OCarm), and Merton College, 319 (written by John Holt OCarm) (for which, see Harvey, ‘Netter manuscripts’, 148–63).
decoDesc.decoNote: Here, there are seven very fine historiated initials, for the prologue and six of the sacraments, there being no initial for the start of De eucharistia (3r, Prologue; 207v, Baptism; 239v, Confirmation; 248v, Ordination; 279v, Marriage; 289v, Confession; 352r, Last Rites, excised). They bear relation stylistically, and to a lesser extent iconographically, to BnF lat. 3378. Kathleen Scott has identified three illustrators at work in our manuscript, of different abilities (Scott, 2. 188). The first initial, appropriately for the start of the manuscript, was by the master artist (Illuminator A), fol. 3r. On a gold ground, the Virgin and Child are enthroned, five Carmelites kneeling before them (white robe over brown habit); the friar on the left is Thomas Netter for he wears a pileus, or academic cap, and is holding an open book; Mary smiles on him and the Christ child reaches out in his direction. Scott describes this artist’s style as ‘soft with much use of a C-curve in his drawing of arms, drapery, body forms, and even in the disposition of figures’. This is the only initial to have a gold ground. The next two initials, for the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation (207v, 239v), are by a second artist (Illustrator B, who shares characteristics with the artist of BnF lat. 3378), which have ‘brighter colouring and crisper outlines; faces are slightly triangular in shape and rendered in pale orange with a moderately heavy application of white’. In the first, a priest standing behind a font with foliate pedestal holds the hand of an infant held by a man in orange robes on the right of the frame, with a noblewoman in a green gown on the left; on a dark blue ground with intricate gold filigree. A Carmelite friar watches the scene from within the foliage of the border bar. In the second initial by this artist, a man and a woman present a swaddled infant to a bishop for Confirmation (expressing the earliest time possible for the administration of the sacrament). The bishop’s mitre is painted gold; the layfolk are again attired as nobles; the group stands beneath an architectural canopy tinted green, perhaps representing the cathedral door since there is also grass here. Against the initial in the margin is a stork, probably the work of the border artist. The man’s face resembles more the work of Illustrator C, who was responsible for the other initials: his figures ‘are shapeless, with faces either smudgy or overly outlined’. On 248v, the sacrament of Ordination is represented by a bishop at an altar, laying a hand on two candidates kneeling either side, one with chalice (sub-deacon), the other with book (deacon), a priest behind. They stand in a vaulted architectural setting with round-headed lancet windows to the rear, whose glazing is suggested by crimson with a gold filigree over; gold is also used for the mitre, frontal and chalice. The initial on 279v for the sacrament of Marriage shows a group under a green canopy fringed with yellow and backed with orange chased with foliage motifs. A priest joins the right hands of a nobleman and noblewoman wearing a golden headdress (crespine), a witness standing behind her. The ground is crimson with gold filigree. On 289v, for the sacrament of Confession, a seated priest, his head covered by a cowl, confesses a kneeling man, a waiting penitent behind, on a ground of crimson and gold filigree. In Scott’s opinion, this artist’s Confession scene ‘is one of the most ill-drawn miniatures in a fifteenth-century manuscript’ (Scott, 2. 188). The final miniature in this cycle, for the sacrament of Last Rites on 352r, is excised. A modern pencil note on 1r states that the initial had already gone in 1952.

The painted borders are particularly fine. The artist has been recognized in Magdalen 157 and in the partial borders of BnF lat. 3378, while the same style of border, but probably a different hand, is in Merton 319. Since this border style seems to be found only in manuscripts of the Doctrinale, Scott has named the craftsman responsible the ‘Netter Master’, his core work belonging to this manuscript and Magdalen 157. Initials are boxed across the width of their columns, with the other letters of the first word fitted vertically at the edge of the box in decorated red and blue lombards. Finials in the margins are scrolling acanthus leaves using a bright palette of orange, green, blue, and mauve. A solid border of blue and gold bars with sprays at intervals, and sprays at head and foot with leaves, elongated green lobes, terminal four-petalled flowers and gold balls. The royal arms (new style) are painted on 3r above the initial.

Beyond the absence of decoration for the beginning of De eucharistia, the decorative hierarchy is regular, and observes first in rank the historiated initials with border decoration; also richly decorated are the two four-line initials for the dedicatory epistles on 2r, which are done in shell gold and are tightly boxed with foliate infill and grounds of green, white, red and purple.

A stylish, eight-line penworked initial S is found at the start of the text proper on 18r. Since this is introductory text, the initial stands outside the iconographic scheme of the rest of the manuscript. It is parted, blue for the bowl above and red below, with foliate infill in reserve, done in red ink above and mauve below. Cusped J-bars run down the entire inner margin with a penwork spray at the foot and the words ‘De sacramentis’ in flourished lombards of red and blue across the head. In the rest of the manuscript, chapters begin with three-line initials, separate doctrinae in the prologue with two-line initials, and initials for in-text citations of authorities are done on the line but enlarged. All these are blue lombards with red flourishing to an extent commensurate with their hierarchical weighting. The penwork is exceptionally skilful and involves decorative infill of acanthus motifs in reserve, extensions into the margin and delicate spraywork north and south. The same man added the running heads, of the form ‘De | Baptismo’ separated across the opening. These use blue lombards for the first letter in each word, duly flourished, and simple red ink for the other letters; flourishing around these initials in the headline is sometimes abandoned. This penman came last to the manuscript, for his work is fitted in around the border decoration, as with his running head ‘Prologus’ on 3r, which accommodates itself to the pre-existent spraywork. His work is also found in BnF MS lat. 2473, another manuscript written by Reginald Westayker.

additions.p: Marks of use on the pages are very infrequent and never extensive, as if annotators have been inhibited by the manuscript’s prestigious pages. The first set of marginal additions made are scribal, where a clause has been omitted through eyeskip, the text marked for insertion with a red lne, as on 18r, 77v, 303r, 345r. These additions are separately ruled and written small.
There are inked crosses of various types and a thin manicule at 24vb.
An early seventeenth-century reader made a note of contents on 1v: ‘Istud est 2m volumen contra wiclevistas . ex prologo’.

The manuscript was handled by the Oxford scholar and chancellor Thomas Gascoigne (1404–1458), a reader in Lincoln’s library, who wrote his familiar invocation of ‘: ihc : ma :’ (for ‘Ihesus Maria’, often cropped), at the head of 5v, 246r, 300v, 301v, 307r–v, 313v, 315r, 359v. He left a brief note on 8r, ‘scilicet papa gregorius .xij.’, identifying an authority, and three more extensive notes, including one on the death of Humfrey Duke of Gloucester, on a blank leaf at the back (see above, fol. 359v). Gascoigne was much influenced by Thomas Netter’s Doctrinale, which emphasizes patristic authority in theological argument. The extent of Gascoigne’s commitment to patrisitc interpretation was exceptional even for his day, and brought him very close to Netter’s position. There is an unusual nota mark on 171v, against a passage in which the author discusses works of Robert Grosseteste on light and colours, and refers to a book from Grosseteste’s study which he had seen in the library of the Greyfriars at Oxford, containing marginal notes ‘de manu magni lincolniensis’. The mark itself is a dot and circle in black ink encircled in red, with a pendant red line connecting to a wavy star like an asterisk, also done in black and red ink. It serves as both a marker for the passage and an illustration of the point being made in the text: ‘Nota quod diuidi possunt accidentia a subiecto et lux a colore cum longo tractu et in fine eius stellam signatam’. The device may be merely illustrative of the text—and the use of red and black together would suggest it is scribal since the scribes did their own rubrication. The passage’s interest, however, in the works of Robert Grosseteste and the status of his books at the Oxford Greyfriars connects firmly to Thomas Gascoigne, who was a friend to the convent and was, indeed, made a present of some of the friars’ books, at least two of which he subsequently gave to Lincoln College (see Lat. 33, 54).

binding.p: By Roger Barnes of Oxford (d. 1631), a binding of the 1620s of reverse calf over pulpboard. Decoration on both boards is restricted to a rectilinear pattern of intersecting lines. Three-line blind fillets to the edges crossing unmitred at the corners, otherwise unembellished. There is extensive worming to both boards at the edges. The spine is split at the upper board. Sewn on eight double thongs of whittawed leather, raised at the spine; only bands 1, 3, 5, 8 are laced into the board. Endbands of undyed thread over what may be a core of rolled paper are non-structural. No fore-edge ties. Fore-edges are sprinkled red. Marks of the early-modern chain-clip are double, one near the head and one near the foot of the fore-edge of the upper board. There are chain-staple marks from an earlier binding on the verso of the back leaf at the centre of the foot, corresponding to the chaining position used in the medieval College. These are three verdigris marks made by the nails, in a span of 66 mm. They are on a pasted strip of parchment, c. 35 × 95 mm, added as protection against the metalwork on the facing board. Flyleaves of original parchment at front and back were formerly pastedown, but probably not in the present binding. The upper flyleaf is creased and pleated. Extensive signs of worming from the medieval binding, upper and lower leaves, separate patterning to the wormholes in the present boards.

history.provenance: The manuscript is of the highest quality, physically as well as textually. In the judgement of Kathleen Scott, ‘this production was physically—in size and material, in quality of script and page layout, and in elegance of decoration—among the finest known monastic productions of the fifteenth century’ (Scott, 2. 189). The scribe was Reginald Westakyr, a Carmelite friar, judged to be a brother of Thomas Netter’s own convent in London: the parchment seems to be of London manufacture, and the early date of the copy would argue for proximity to the author. Netter was putting the finishing touches to this second part of the work early in 1426, when Pope Martin V received a copy of the first. A copy of the second part was sent to the pope the following year: Martin acknowledged it on 8 August 1427 and wrote that he had had it read and approved between 17 June and 23 July (see Harvey, ‘Diffusion of the Doctrinale’, 281–2, and A. Hudson in ODNB). The work was disseminated in England in the fifteenth century through a programme of copying organized by members of the Carmelite order. Of the fifteen surviving copies of the Doctrinale made in England, eleven have signs of production by Carmelites and eight contain one or more illustration. The prestigious finish of these copies reveals the order’s perception of the work’s value as well as the possible status of these volumes as presentation copies. Certainly, the presence of the royal arms in our manuscript, painted above the first illuminated initial, seeks explanation. Books I to IV of the work were composed at the behest of King Henry V, who chose Netter as his confessor in 1413. After the king’s death on 31 August 1422, Netter became spiritual counsellor to the child Henry VI. But it seems unlikely that our copy was intended for Henry since Lincoln’s Founder, Bishop Richard Flemming, acquired it so close to its time of writing, either during Netter’s lifetime or shortly after Netter’s death on 2 November 1430. (Flemming’s own death followed shortly after, in January 1431.) Perhaps the royal arms were taken over from an exemplar scheme and are merely complimentary in referring to the original royal commission.

Inscriptions at the front of the volume may help to clarify the sequence of events by which the manuscript came to the College: one states that the book was the Founder’s gift, ‘ex dono’; the other, on the title-piece, states that it came by bequest, ‘ex legato’. It is possible that Flemming had stood patron but died before the manuscript was completed, hence the judgement that it had been bequeathed. Such an ambitious statement of Catholic orthodoxy as is set out in the Doctrinale would certainly have found a natural place in Flemming’s fledgling college, founded to combat the evangelical challenge of Wycliffism. This part of the work explained the sacraments, which chimes with a requirement in the oath of admission to fellowship, as recited in the statutes, to defend the sacraments. The manuscript, described as a gift of the Founder, was reported for the library in 1474, when it was chained to the second desk on the south side of the room, in company with biblical commentaries: ‘Item in 2a parte eiusdem disci Walden’ contra Wiclyf ex dono fundatoris, 2o fo. prologus’ (A1. 25).

Labels and marks: The medieval title-piece from the lower board of the medieval binding has been pasted in at the head of fol. 1v. In the primary Textura it reads, ‘Walden’ contra Wyclefe . Ex legato | M’ Ricardi Flemmyng quondam | Episcopi Lincoln’ ac fundatoris huius | Collegii.’ At the centre of the same page is an ex libris of slightly earlier date: ‘Liber Collegii lincoln’ ex dono Magistri Ricardi Flemmyng quondam Episcopi lincoln’ ac fundatoris antedicti Collegii’. At the head of this page is the mark of omission made by Gerard Langbaine to signal that he could not find the work in James, Ecloga. In black ink on the fore-edge is the numeral ‘77’. The early-modern press-mark ‘E. 4. 12’ is in the top corner of 1r. The College bookplate of 1703 is pasted towards the foot of 1v. Beneath it is pencilled the modern Bodleian shelf-mark, ‘MS. Linc. Coll. (b) Lat. 106’. On the inside of the upper board is boldly pencilled ‘MSS. Arch. 2’, probably nineteenth century. Vestiges of the paper label around the fore-edge near the head of the upper board. On the spine, the usual square paper labels: at the head, the small, square label with a printed numeral 2; at the foot, the pale blue Bodleian printed label, mostly rubbed away.
